name: Lead-based ceruse
lead: Ceruse, also called Venetian ceruse or white lead, was a cosmetic paste of lead carbonate used for centuries to whiten the face and cover blemishes, scars and freckles, often prepared with vinegar.[1] Pale skin signalled wealth and leisure in the societies that used it, since outdoor labourers tanned.[1]

Repeated application allowed lead to be absorbed through the skin, and historical accounts describe poisoning, organ damage and death among users.[1] It is no longer a legitimate cosmetic; the World Health Organization listed lead as a major chemical of concern in cosmetics in 2010.[1]
infobox: Lead-based white pigment, often mixed with vinegar[1]
Antiquity to the 18th century and later[1]

paras: Lead-based whitening is described as beginning in ancient Rome, with similar white cosmetics in Egypt and Greece.[1] From the 14th century Italy, especially Venice, exported ceruse, and the Venetian product was regarded as the finest and sold at a premium.[1] A 16th-century method used lead sheets, vinegar and sealed clay pots, and a 1688 recipe described ceruse as water, vinegar and lead.[1]

Elizabeth I of England is often named as a user, though the Wikipedia article notes that historians disagree and the evidence is limited.[1] Isabella d'Este was described in 1534 as heavily made up, and Maria Coventry, Countess of Coventry, is believed to have died of lead poisoning in 1760, earning the nickname "Death by Vanity".[1]

Accounts describe abdominal pain, nausea, high blood pressure, reduced fertility, confusion and convulsions from lead absorbed through the skin.[1] The paste could also mottle, peel and scar the skin, which led users to apply further layers, producing a cycle of dependence.[1] Hair loss at the hairline may have helped shape the fashion for high foreheads.[1] Scientific studies confirmed lead's dangers only at the end of the 18th century.[1]

card.summary: A historical lead-based white face paste that whitened skin and poisoned its users.
card.note: Contains lead; documented to cause lead poisoning.

quick.overview:
Ceruse was a white paste made from lead, used from antiquity to the 18th century to give a pale complexion and cover blemishes. Venetian ceruse was the most prized version.

It is a historical practice rather than a current product, documented here because it is a well-known example of a lightening agent with serious harms.
quick.mechanism: The paste was applied to the face as an opaque white cover, with lead-containing pigment suspended in vinegar or similar carriers. It masked skin tone rather than altering melanin.
quick.risks: Historical accounts describe lead poisoning from skin absorption, with abdominal pain, organ damage, convulsions and death, plus skin damage that led to heavier application. The WHO lists lead as a major cosmetic chemical of concern.
